What is Ruby: Ruby is a dynamic, interpreted, reflective, object-oriented programming language created by Yukihiro Matsumoto (Matz) in 1995. It combines syntax inspired by Perl and Smalltalk with object-oriented features. Everything in Ruby is an object — even integers and booleans. Ruby follows the Principle of Least Surprise (POLS), meaning the language behaves as you'd expect. It's known for its elegant syntax, powerful metaprogramming, and the Ruby on Rails web framework.

# Install: ruby --version
# Run: ruby file.rb

puts "Hello from Ruby!"

# Everything is an object
puts 42.class       # Integer
puts true.class     # TrueClass
puts "hi".class     # String
puts nil.class      # NilClass

# Interactive: irb
Ruby Syntax & Conventions: Ruby uses English-like, minimalist syntax. Parentheses are optional for method calls. Blocks defined with do/end or {}. Class and method names follow conventions: SNAKE_CASE for files/variables, CamelCase for classes, snake_case for methods. Files end with .rb. Comments use # for single line and =begin/=end for multi-line. Indentation is 2 spaces (convention, not enforced).

# Naming conventions
file_name = "example.rb"
class UserProfile
end

def calculate_total
  # 2-space indentation
  puts "calculating..."
end

# Optional parentheses
puts "Hello"
puts("Hello")  # same

# Multiline comment
=begin
This is a
multiline comment
=end
Variables & Types: Ruby is dynamically typed. Local variables (name), instance variables (@name), class variables (@@name), global variables ($name), and constants (NAME). Basic types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, Boolean, Nil. Type checking occurs at runtime — no static type declarations needed. Symbols (:name) are immutable, lightweight identifiers used for keys and method names.

name = "Alice"       # local variable (string)
@name = "Bob"         # instance variable
@@count = 0           # class variable
$debug = true         # global variable
MAX_SIZE = 100         # constant (warning if reassigned)

# Types
age = 30              # Integer
pi = 3.14             # Float
flag = true           # TrueClass / FalseClass
nothing = nil         # NilClass
sym = :ruby           # Symbol

puts name.class       # String
puts sym.class        # Symbol
Strings & Interpolation: Ruby strings can be single-quoted (no interpolation) or double-quoted (supports interpolation and escape sequences). #{expression} interpolates any Ruby expression. Strings are mutable. Common methods: length, upcase, downcase, capitalize, reverse, split, join, gsub, strip, include?, empty?. << or + for concatenation.

name = "Ruby"
age = 30

# String interpolation (double quotes only)
puts "Hello, #{name}!"       # Hello, Ruby!
puts "Age: #{age}"           # Age: 30
puts "Pi: #{Math::PI.round(2)}"  # Pi: 3.14

# Single quotes = literal
puts 'Hello, #{name}!'       # Hello, #{name}!

# Common methods
puts "hello".upcase         # HELLO
puts "hello".capitalize     # Hello
puts "a,b,c".split(",")    # ["a", "b", "c"]
puts "hello".include?("ll")  # true
Arrays: Arrays are ordered, integer-indexed collections. Can hold mixed types. Index starts at 0. Negative indices count from end (-1 = last). Common methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, first, last, length/ size, include?, empty?, sort, reverse, join, map/collect, select/filter, reject, each, each_with_index. Arrays created with [] or Array.new.

arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
puts arr[0]        # 1
puts arr[-1]       # 5
puts arr[1..3].join(", ")  # "2, 3, 4"

# Mixed types
mixed = [1, "two", :three, 4.0]

# Common operations
arr << 6           # append
arr.push(7)        # also append
last = arr.pop     # remove last
first = arr.shift  # remove first

# Iteration
arr.each { |n| puts n }
arr.each_with_index { |n, i| puts "#{i}: #{n}" }

# Transform
squares = arr.map { |n| n ** 2 }
Hashes: Hashes are key-value dictionaries. Keys can be any object type, but symbols are most common (memory efficient, immutable). Two syntaxes: hash-rocket (=>) for any key type, and JSON-style for symbol keys (Ruby 1.9+). Default values can be set. Common methods: keys, values, key?, has_key?, has_value?, fetch, merge, select, each, except, slice.

# Hash with symbol keys (modern syntax)
person = { name: "Alice", age: 30, city: "NYC" }
puts person[:name]     # Alice

# Hash-rocket syntax (any key type)
old = { "name" => "Bob", :key => "value", 1 => "one" }

# Default value
counts = Hash.new(0)   # default 0
counts[:a] += 1        # counts[:a] = 1
puts counts[:b]        # 0 (default)

# Iteration
person.each { |key, val| puts "#{key}: #{val}" }

# Merging
merged = person.merge({ age: 31, country: "US" })

# Selection
adults = { alice: 30, bob: 15, charlie: 25 }.select { |_, age| age >= 18 }
Symbols: Symbols are immutable, reusable identifiers represented as :name. Unlike strings, every instance of a symbol with the same name refers to the same object in memory (same object_id). This makes them ideal for hash keys and method references. Symbols are not garbage collected, so be careful about creating them dynamically from user input. Convert: to_sym / intern, to_s.

:name          # symbol literal
:"with spaces"  # quoted symbol
:"my_var"       # symbol with special chars

# Symbols are singletons
puts "name".object_id == "name".object_id  # false (different strings)
puts :name.object_id == :name.object_id      # true (same symbol)

# Common usage
person = { name: "Alice", age: 30 }

# Conversion
sym = "hello".to_sym   # :hello
str = :hello.to_s      # "hello"

# Method as symbol
objects = [1, "a", 2, "b"]
objects.select(&:to_s)  # shorthand for { |o| o.to_s }

Local & Global Variables: Ruby variables are dynamically typed. Local variables start with a lowercase letter or _, instance variables with @, class variables with @@, and global variables with $. Understanding scope rules prevents subtle bugs. Local vars are scoped to the current block/method; instance vars belong to an object instance; class vars are shared across the hierarchy; globals are visible everywhere (avoid when possible).

name = 'Alice'          # local variable
@count = 0               # instance variable
@@total = 0              # class variable
$debug = true            # global variable

puts defined?(name)      # 'local-variable'
Constants: Constants in Ruby start with a capital letter. They are not truly immutable — Ruby warns but doesn't prevent reassignment. Use them for values that logically shouldn't change.

PI = 3.14159
MAX_USERS = 100

# Ruby warns on reassignment
PI = 3.14  # warning: already initialized constant PI
Data Types: Ruby's core types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, true/false (TrueClass/FalseClass), nil (NilClass). Everything is an object — even nil has methods.

puts 42.class          # Integer
puts 3.14.class        # Float
puts 'hello'.class     # String
puts :symbol.class     # Symbol
puts true.class        # TrueClass
puts nil.class         # NilClass

puts 42.to_s           # '42' — Integer#to_s
Type Conversion: Ruby provides explicit conversion methods: to_s, to_i, to_f, to_a, to_sym. Implicit conversion is rare — Ruby prefers raising errors to silent coercion.

age = '25'
puts age.to_i + 5      # 30
puts '3.14'.to_f       # 3.14
puts 42.to_s           # '42'
puts :hello.to_s       # 'hello'

# No implicit conversion
# '5' + 3  # TypeError (String + Integer)

Arithmetic: Standard + - * / % ** operators. Integer division truncates toward zero. ** is exponentiation. Ruby also supports shorthand assignment operators (+=, -=, etc.).

puts 10 / 3   # 3 (integer division)
puts 10 / 3.0 # 3.333...
puts 2 ** 10  # 1024
puts 10 % 3   # 1

x = 5
x += 3        # 8
Comparison: == != < > <= >=. Ruby also has .eql? (type-sensitive comparison) and .equal? (object identity comparison). <=> (spaceship operator) returns -1 if left is less, 0 if equal, 1 if greater.

puts 5 == 5.0   # true (value equality)
puts 5.eql?(5.0) # false (type-sensitive)
puts 5 <=> 10   # -1
puts 10 <=> 10  # 0
puts 10 <=> 5   # 1
Logical: && || ! (and or not). and/or/not have lower precedence than &&/||/!. Short-circuit evaluation applies — && stops on first false, || stops on first true. Ruby uses truthiness (everything except nil and false is truthy).

puts true && false  # false
puts false || 42    # 42
puts !true          # false

# Low-precedence versions (use with caution)
puts true and false  # true (prints true, then evaluates false)
puts (true and false) # false

# Short-circuit
name = nil
display_name = name || "Guest"  # "Guest"
Range: Ruby ranges: inclusive (..) and exclusive (...). Used in iteration, slicing arrays, and case conditions. Ranges can be created from any comparable objects.

range = 1..5
puts range.to_a    # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

excl = 1...5
puts excl.to_a    # [1, 2, 3, 4]

case score
when 90..100 then 'A'
when 80...90 then 'B'
end

# Range with strings
puts ('a'..'e').to_a  # ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

if/unless/elsif: Ruby uses if, elsif, else, unless, and ternary (?:). unless is the opposite of if and reads naturally for negative conditions. if/unless can be used as statement modifiers (postfix). All conditionals return a value. Only nil and false are falsy — everything else (including 0, empty strings, empty arrays) is truthy.

age = 20

if age >= 18
  puts "Adult"
elsif age >= 13
  puts "Teen"
else
  puts "Child"
end

# unless (opposite of if)
unless age < 18
  puts "Can vote"
end

# Statement modifiers (postfix)
puts "Adult" if age >= 18
puts "Minor" unless age >= 18

# Ternary
type = age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor"

# Truthiness
if 0       # truthy! (unlike some languages)
  puts "zero is truthy"
end

if ""     # also truthy
  puts "empty string is truthy"
end
case/when: Ruby's case/when is more flexible than switch/case in other languages. It uses === (case equality operator) for comparison, which can match classes, regexp, ranges, and procs. when can have multiple values separated by commas. else is the default. Returns the value of the last evaluated expression.

grade = 85

result = case grade
when 90..100 then "A"
when 80...90 then "B"
when 70...80 then "C"
when 60...70 then "D"
else "F"
end

puts result  # B

# === operator matching
case "Hello"
when String then puts "It's a string"
when /^H/ then puts "Starts with H"
end

# Multiple values
case 3
when 1, 3, 5 then puts "Odd single digit"
when 2, 4, 6 then puts "Even single digit"
end
while/until Loops: while executes while condition is truthy. until executes while condition is falsy (opposite of while). Both can be used as statement modifiers. begin/end versions guarantee at least one execution. Loop control: break (exit loop), next (skip iteration), redo (rerun current iteration), retry (restart from beginning).

# while
x = 0
while x < 5
  puts x
  x += 1
end

# until
y = 0
until y == 5
  puts y
  y += 1
end

# Statement modifiers
i = 0
puts i += 1 while i < 5

# begin/end (do at least once)
z = 10
begin
  puts z
  z += 1
end while z < 5  # runs once

# Loop control
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].each do |n|
  next if n.even?  # skip evens
  break if n > 4    # stop at 5
  puts n
end
for/in & each: Ruby has for/in loops but they're rarely used — each and friends are preferred. for/in iterates over enumerables but doesn't create a new scope for the variable (leaks it). each and the Enumerable module provide a rich set of iteration methods with proper scoping. Range literals (1..10) are commonly used for iteration.

# for loop (rarely idiomatic)
for i in 1..5
  puts i
end
puts i  # i leaks! (5)

# each (idiomatic)
(1..5).each { |i| puts i }

# each with index
%w[a b c].each_with_index { |v, i| puts "#{i}: #{v}" }

# Times, upto, downto, step
3.times { puts "hi" }
1.upto(5) { |n| puts n }
5.downto(1) { |n| puts n }
0.step(10, 2) { |n| puts n }  # 0, 2, 4, ..., 10

# Ranges
(1..5).to_a    # [1,2,3,4,5] (inclusive)
(1...5).to_a   # [1,2,3,4] (exclusive)

Defining Methods: Methods defined with def/end. Parentheses optional. Return last evaluated expression implicitly or use explicit return. Method names can end with ? (predicates, return boolean), ! (dangerous/mutating version), = (setter). Arguments can have default values. Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) for named parameters. Splat (*) captures multiple args. Double splat (**) captures keyword args.

# Implicit return (last expression)
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

# Explicit return
def max(a, b)
  return a if a > b
  b
end

# Default arguments
def greet(name = "World")
  "Hello, #{name}!"
end

# Keyword arguments
def configure(host:, port: 3000, debug: false)
  puts "#{host}:#{port} (debug=#{debug})"
end

configure(host: "localhost")  # localhost:3000
configure(host: "app", port: 8080, debug: true)

# Splat

def sum(*numbers)
  numbers.sum
end

puts sum(1, 2, 3, 4)  # 10

# Predicate methods (end with ?)
puts [].empty?        # true
puts 5.odd?           # true

# Bang methods (end with !)
name = "ruby"
name.upcase!          # modifies in place
puts name             # RUBY
Splat & Keyword Arguments: Ruby methods support flexible argument patterns. Splat (*) captures multiple positional arguments into an array. Double splat (**) captures keyword arguments into a hash. Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) provide named parameters with optional defaults. Arguments can have default values. The order is: positional, optional, splat, keyword, double splat, block (&).
Method Visibility (public/private/protec: Ruby methods have three visibility levels. public — called by anyone (default). private — only callable without a receiver (self implicit). protected — callable within the same class hierarchy, even from different instances. private and protected are declared with `private`/`protected` keywords or by listing method names as symbols after the keyword. Unlike some languages, Ruby's private is more like "internal".

class Person
  def initialize(name, age)
    @name = name
    @age = age
  end

  # Public by default
  def introduce
    "Hi, I'm #{@name}"
  end

  # Protected — can be called by other instances of same class
  def age
    @age
  end

  def older_than?(other)
    age > other.age  # protected allows cross-instance call
  end

private

  def secret
    "shh!"
  end
  # Or: private :secret

protected :age
end
Method Aliases & Undef: alias creates a copy of a method under a new name. alias_method does the same (preferred in modules). undef removes a method (prevents inheritance). Useful for method decoration, AOP, and library design.

class Greeter
  def hello
    "Hello!"
  end
  alias hi hello  # hi is now an alias for hello

  def greet(name)
    "Hello, #{name}!"
  end
  alias_method :greeting, :greet
end

g = Greeter.new
puts g.hello  # "Hello!"
puts g.hi     # "Hello!" (same method)

# undef — removes method
class SilentGreeter < Greeter
  undef hello  # removes hello method
  undef_method :greet  # removes greet method
end

Classes & Objects: Ruby is pure object-oriented. Classes defined with class/end. Constructor is initialize. Instance variables (@name) are private by default. attr_reader, attr_writer, attr_accessor create getters/setters automatically. self refers to the current object. Class methods defined with self.method_name. Every class inherits from Object (which inherits from BasicObject).

class Person
  # Attribute shortcuts
  attr_reader :name     # getter only
  attr_accessor :age    # getter + setter

  # Constructor
  def initialize(name, age = 0)
    @name = name
    @age = age
  end

  # Instance method
  def introduce
    "Hi, I'm #{@name}, age #{@age}"
  end

  # Class method
  def self.species
    "Homo sapiens"
  end

  # Custom setter
  def name=(value)
    raise "Invalid name" if value.nil? || value.empty?
    @name = value
  end
end

# Usage
alice = Person.new("Alice", 30)
puts alice.introduce       # Hi, I'm Alice, age 30
puts alice.name            # Alice (via attr_reader)
alice.age = 31             # (via attr_accessor)
puts Person.species        # Homo sapiens
Inheritance: Ruby supports single inheritance with the < operator. Modules provide multiple inheritance-like behavior via mixins. super calls the parent method with the same arguments. Method resolution order (MRO) follows the lookup path: object -> class -> modules (reverse order of include) -> superclass. ancestor chain shows inheritance.

class Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} makes a sound"
  end

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
end

class Dog < Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} barks!"
  end

  def wag_tail
    "#{@name} wags tail"
  end
end

class Cat < Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} meows"
  end
end

dog = Dog.new("Rex")
cat = Cat.new("Whiskers")
puts dog.speak   # Rex barks!
puts cat.speak   # Whiskers meows
puts dog.wag_tail  # Rex wags tail

# Ancestor chain
puts Dog.ancestors.inspect
# Dog, Animal, Object, Kernel, BasicObject
Modules & Mixins: Modules collect methods and constants. They cannot be instantiated. Use include for instance methods (mixins), extend for class methods, and prepend to override methods (prepended module methods are called first). Namespacing: MyModule::MyClass. The include lookup checks modules in reverse order of inclusion. Enumerable and Comparable are built-in mixin examples.

module Greetable
  def greet
    "Hello, I'm #{@name}"
  end
end

module Walkable
  def walk
    "#{@name} is walking"
  end
end

class Robot
  include Greetable
  include Walkable

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
end

robot = Robot.new("R2D2")
puts robot.greet  # Hello, I'm R2D2
puts robot.walk   # R2D2 is walking

# extend (class methods)
module ClassMethods
  def version
    "1.0"
  end
end

class App
  extend ClassMethods
end

puts App.version  # 1.0

# Namespacing
module Admin
  class User
    def role = "admin"
  end
end

user = Admin::User.new
puts user.role
attr_accessor/reader/writer Deep Dive: attr_reader, attr_writer, and attr_accessor are metaprogramming shortcuts that define getter/setter methods. attr_reader defines a getter (@name → name), attr_writer defines a setter (name=), attr_accessor defines both. They accept multiple symbols. These are class-level methods (Class.attr_reader) that dynamically define instance methods using define_method.
Method Resolution Order (MRO): Ruby's method lookup follows a strict path: singleton class → class → included modules (reverse order) → superclass → ... → BasicObject. The `ancestors` method shows this path. `singleton_class` is the class of a single object. prepend inserts a module before the class in the lookup. Understanding MRO is crucial for debugging unexpected method calls.

module A
  def greet; "A"; end
end

module B
  def greet; "B"; end
end

class Parent
  def greet; "Parent"; end
end

class Child < Parent
  include A
  include B  # B comes before A in lookup
end

puts Child.ancestors.inspect
# Child, B, A, Parent, Object, Kernel, BasicObject
puts Child.new.greet  # "B" (finds B first)

# prepend — inserts before the class
class Child2 < Parent
  prepend A
end

puts Child2.ancestors.inspect
# A, Child2, Parent, Object, Kernel, BasicObject
Singleton Methods & Eigenclass: Ruby allows defining methods on individual objects (singleton methods). These live in the object's eigenclass (singleton class). def obj.method or class << self syntax. Class methods are really singleton methods on the class object. Eigenclasses are invisible but discoverable via singleton_class. This is fundamental to Ruby's object model.

obj = "hello"

# Singleton method on one object
def obj.shout
  upcase + "!"
end

puts obj.shout  # "HELLO!"
other = "world"
# other.shout  # NoMethodError

# Class << self (opens eigenclass)
class << obj
  def whisper
    downcase + "..."
  end
end

puts obj.whisper  # "hello..."

# Eigenclass of an object
puts obj.singleton_class  # #<Class:#<String:0x...>>

# Class methods are singleton methods on the class object
class MyClass
  class << self
    def class_method
      "class method"
    end
  end
end

puts MyClass.class_method  # "class method"

Enumerable Module: Enumerable is Ruby's most powerful mixin. Include it + define each and you get map, select, reject, reduce, any?, all?, none?, one?, count, group_by, partition, sort_by, first, take, drop, min, max, min_by, max_by, each_slice, each_cons, cycle, detect/find, grep, flat_map, zip, chunk, and many more. Lazy enumerators (lazy) for infinite sequences.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Map / Collect
squares = numbers.map { |n| n ** 2 }

# Select / Find all
evens = numbers.select(&:even?)  # [2, 4]

# Reject
odds = numbers.reject(&:even?)   # [1, 3, 5]

# Reduce / Inject
sum = numbers.reduce(0) { |acc, n| acc + n }  # 15
# Or shorter:
sum = numbers.reduce(:+)  # 15

# Any? / All? / None?
puts numbers.any?(&:even?)   # true
puts numbers.all? { |n| n > 0 }  # true

# Group by
by_parity = numbers.group_by(&:even?)
# { false => [1,3,5], true => [2,4] }

# Each slice
numbers.each_slice(2) { |slice| puts slice.inspect }
# [1, 2]
# [3, 4]
# [5]

# Lazy enumeration
infinite = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .select(&:even?)
  .first(5)
# [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
Arrays Deep: Beyond basic array operations, Ruby provides powerful methods: combination, permutation, product, zip, transpose, flatten, uniq, difference (&), union (|), sample, shuffle, rotate, cycle, bsearch, pack. Many accept blocks for advanced transformations.

arr = [1, 2, 3]

# Combinations & permutations
arr.combination(2).to_a  # [[1,2], [1,3], [2,3]]
arr.permutation(2).to_a  # [[1,2], [1,3], [2,1], [2,3], [3,1], [3,2]]
arr.product([4, 5])      # [[1,4], [1,5], [2,4], [2,5], [3,4], [3,5]]

# Zip
a = [1, 2]; b = ['a', 'b']
a.zip(b)  # [[1, "a"], [2, "b"]]

# Set-like operations
[1, 2, 3] & [2, 3, 4]  # [2, 3] (intersection)
[1, 2, 3] | [3, 4, 5]  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (union)
[1, 2, 3] - [2]         # [1, 3] (difference)

# Sampling & shuffling
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].sample(2)  # random selection
[1, 2, 3].shuffle           # random order

# Binary search (sorted arrays)
[1, 3, 5, 7, 9].bsearch { |x| x >= 5 }  # 5
Hashes Deep: Hashes support advanced features: default procs (compute defaults dynamically), fetch with block (safe access), transform_keys/transform_values (bulk conversion), slice/except (subselection), dig (nested access), compact (remove nil values). The merge method accepts a block for conflict resolution.
Sets: Set implements a collection of unique values. It requires `require 'set'`. Sets provide mathematical set operations: union (+ or |), intersection (&), difference (-), subset?/superset?/disjoint? Also: add, delete, include?, each, map (returns array). Sets ensure uniqueness unlike arrays.

require 'set'

set1 = Set.new([1, 2, 3])
set2 = Set.new([3, 4, 5])

# Set operations
puts set1 | set2   # #<Set: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}>  (union)
puts set1 & set2   # #<Set: {3}>              (intersection)
puts set1 - set2   # #<Set: {1, 2}>           (difference)

# Comparison
set1.subset?(set2)   # false
Set[1, 2].subset?(set1)  # true
set1.disjoint?(set2) # false

# Auto-deduplication
Set.new([1, 1, 2, 2, 3])  # #<Set: {1, 2, 3}>
Enumerable Chaining & Lazy: Enumerable methods can be chained for expressive data pipelines. Each method returns a new Enumerable. Lazy enumeration (Enumerator::Lazy) defers computation until needed — useful for large or infinite collections. Use .lazy to create a lazy enumerator, then force evaluation with .to_a, .first, or .each.

# Method chaining
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  .select(&:odd?)
  .map { |n| n ** 2 }
  .reject { |n| n < 10 }
  .each { |n| puts n }

# Lazy enumeration — processes on demand
big_data = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .select(&:even?)
  .map { |n| n * n }
  .first(5)
puts big_data.inspect  # [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

# Lazy file processing
lines = File.foreach("big_file.txt").lazy
  .map(&:chomp)
  .reject(&:empty?)
  .first(100)

# Each with index (returns enumerator if no block)
%w[a b c].each_with_index.map { |v, i| "#{i}: #{v}" }
Enumerator & Generators: Enumerator wraps iteration as an object. Create with Enumerator.new or from methods like each. External iteration with next/rewind/peek/feed. Enumerators can be infinite. Fiber-based generators provide coroutine-like behavior.

# Custom enumerator
gen = Enumerator.new do |y|
  y << 1
  y << 2
  y << 3
end
puts gen.next  # 1
puts gen.next  # 2
puts gen.peek  # 3 (next without consuming)
puts gen.next  # 3

# Infinite enumerator
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a = b = 1
  loop do
    y << a
    a, b = b, a + b
  end
end
puts fib.first(8).inspect  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21]

# Rewind
gen.rewind
puts gen.next  # 1 again

# From existing method
enum = [1, 2, 3].each  # Enumerator
puts enum.with_index.map { |n, i| n * i }

begin/rescue/ensure: Ruby uses begin/rescue/ensure/else for exception handling. rescue catches exceptions by class. Multiple rescue blocks for different exceptions. ensure always runs (like finally). else runs if no exception. raise/throw to trigger errors. $! contains last exception, $@ contains backtrace. StandardError is the common superclass (most code should rescue StandardError, not Exception).

def divide(a, b)
  begin
    result = a / b
  rescue ZeroDivisionError => e
    puts "Error: #{e.message}"
    nil
  rescue TypeError => e
    puts "Type error: #{e.message}"
    nil
  else
    puts "No error occurred"
    result
  ensure
    puts "This always runs"
  end
end

puts divide(10, 2)  # No error occurred / This always runs / 5
puts divide(10, 0)  # Error: divided by 0 / This always runs / nil

# Inline rescue (risky, catches all StandardError)
value = risky_call() rescue "default"

# Custom exceptions
class MyError < StandardError; end
raise MyError, "Something went wrong"
Custom Exception Classes: Create custom exceptions by subclassing StandardError or its subclasses. Build an exception hierarchy for granular error handling. Each custom class can have its own attributes. Rescue ordering matters — catch most specific exceptions first. Built-in exceptions: RuntimeError, ArgumentError, TypeError, NameError, NoMethodError, IndexError, KeyError.

# Exception hierarchy
class AppError < StandardError; end
class ValidationError < AppError; end
class AuthError < AppError; end
class NotFoundError < AppError; end

# Custom exception with attributes
class ApiError < StandardError
  attr_reader :status_code, :details

  def initialize(message, status_code: 500, details: {})
    @status_code = status_code
    @details = details
    super(message)
  end
end

# Usage
def fetch_user(id)
  raise NotFoundError, "User #{id} not found" if id.nil?
  raise ApiError.new("API timeout", status_code: 503)
end

# Rescue ordering matters
begin
  fetch_user(nil)
rescue NotFoundError => e
  puts "Not found: #{e.message}"
rescue ValidationError => e
  puts "Invalid: #{e.message}"
rescue ApiError => e
  puts "API error #{e.status_code}: #{e.message}"
rescue AppError => e
  puts "General app error: #{e.message}"
end
ensure & else Clauses: ensure always runs regardless of whether an exception occurred — used for cleanup (closing files, releasing locks). else runs only when no exception was raised. rescue without an argument catches StandardError. You can have multiple rescue blocks, one else, and one ensure per begin block.

def process_file(path)
  file = File.open(path, "r")
  begin
    data = file.read
    raise "Bad data" if data.empty?
    data.upcase
  rescue => e
    puts "Error: #{e.message}"
    nil
  else
    puts "Processing succeeded!"  # only if no exception
    data
  ensure
    file.close                    # always closes
    puts "File closed"
  end
end

# Common pattern: ensure for cleanup
def with_lock
  lock = acquire_lock
  begin
    yield
  ensure
    release_lock(lock)  # always released
  end
end
raise vs throw: raise is for exceptions (error conditions). throw/catch is for control flow (not errors). raise creates an exception object that propagates up the call stack. throw with a symbol/label and catch captures it. throw is like a non-local exit — faster but should only be used for control flow, not error handling. catch returns the value passed to throw.

# raise (exceptions)
raise "Something went wrong"                    # RuntimeError
raise ArgumentError, "Invalid argument"         # specific type
raise CustomError.new("Custom message")         # custom

# catch/throw (control flow)
result = catch(:done) do
  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].each do |n|
    throw(:done, "Found #{n}") if n == 3
  end
  "not found"
end
puts result  # "Found 3"

# Practical: early exit from nested loops
catch(:found) do
  matrix.each do |row|
    row.each do |value|
      throw(:found, value) if value == target
    end
  end
end

# Never use throw for error handling — use raise

require/load/autoload: require loads and executes a file once (tracks loaded files in $"). load loads and executes every time (for development). require_relative loads relative to the current file. autoload defers loading until the constant is first referenced (deprecated in Ruby 2.x style, replaced by Zeitwerk in Rails). $LOAD_PATH ($:) contains directories searched by require.

# require — loads once, searches $LOAD_PATH
require "json"
require "set"

# require_relative — relative to current file
require_relative "lib/helper"
require_relative "../config/settings"

# load — executes every time (useful for development)
load "config.rb"

# Custom $LOAD_PATH
$LOAD_PATH << File.expand_path("lib")
require "my_module"

# Check if loaded
puts $".select { |f| f.include?("json") }  # ["json"]

# autoload (deferred loading)
autoload :MyClass, "my_class"
# MyClass is loaded only when first referenced
Gems & Gemfile: rubygems.org hosts Ruby libraries (gems). gem install installs a gem. The Gemfile (Bundler) declares dependencies with version constraints: `>= 1.0`, `~> 2.0` (pessimistic, accepts 2.x), `>= 1.0, < 3.0`. Groups organize gems by environment. `gem "rspec", group: :test`. Common gems: sinatra, rails, rspec, nokogiri, httparty, devise.

# Gemfile
# source "https://rubygems.org"
# 
# gem "sinatra", "~> 3.0"
# gem "puma", ">= 5.0"
# gem "nokogiri"
# 
# group :development, :test do
#   gem "rspec"
#   gem "pry"
# end
# 
# group :production do
#   gem "pg"
# end

# Using gems in code
require "sinatra"
require "httparty"

response = HTTParty.get("https://api.github.com/users/octocat")
puts response["login"]
Bundler Workflow: Bundler manages gem dependencies. `bundle init` creates a Gemfile. `bundle install` installs gems and creates Gemfile.lock. `bundle exec` runs commands with locked gems. `bundle update` updates gems. `bundle outdated` lists outdated gems. Gemfile.lock should be committed to version control for reproducible builds.

# bundle init            # Create Gemfile
# bundle install         # Install gems
# bundle exec ruby app.rb  # Run with locked gems
# bundle update sinatra  # Update specific gem
# bundle outdated        # List outdated gems
# bundle check           # Check all gems installed

# Gemfile.lock ensures consistency across environments
# Always commit Gemfile.lock to version control

# Groups in code
# Bundler.require(:default, :development)

# Gemfile example with git source
# gem "my_gem", git: "https://github.com/user/my_gem.git"
# gem "other", path: "/path/to/local/gem"

Reading & Writing Files: File operations with File class. Block form auto-closes. Modes: r (read), w (write, truncate), a (append), r+ (read/write), w+ (read/write, truncate), a+ (read/append). Binary mode: rb, wb. Common methods: File.read, File.write, File.readlines, File.foreach (memory efficient for large files). Dir for directory operations. Pathname for path manipulation.

# Block form (auto-closes)
File.open("example.txt", "w") do |f|
  f.puts "Line 1"
  f.puts "Line 2"
end

# Simple read/write
content = File.read("example.txt")
puts content

# Read lines into array
lines = File.readlines("example.txt")
puts lines.length

# Memory-efficient line-by-line
File.foreach("example.txt") do |line|
  puts line.chomp  # chomp removes trailing newline
end

# Append
File.write("log.txt", "New entry\n", mode: "a")

# Check existence
puts File.exist?("example.txt")  # true

# Directory operations
Dir.mkdir("mydir") unless Dir.exist?("mydir")
Dir.entries(".").each { |entry| puts entry }
CSV & YAML Parsing: Ruby's standard library includes CSV and YAML modules. CSV.read loads all rows as arrays of strings. CSV.foreach streams rows. CSV.table returns a table with header access. YAML.load_file parses YAML files into Ruby objects (hashes, arrays, etc.). YAML.dump serializes Ruby objects to YAML. Both modules are part of stdlib and need require.

require 'csv'
require 'yaml'

# CSV — reading
CSV.read("data.csv")                    # array of arrays
CSV.foreach("data.csv") do |row|
  puts row[0]  # first column
end

# CSV with headers
CSV.table("data.csv").each do |row|
  puts row[:name]  # access by column name
end

# CSV — writing
CSV.open("output.csv", "w") do |csv|
  csv << ["Name", "Age", "City"]
  csv << ["Alice", 30, "NYC"]
  csv << ["Bob", 25, "SF"]
end

# YAML — reading
config = YAML.load_file("config.yml")
puts config["database"]["host"]

# YAML — dumping
data = { name: "Ruby", version: 3.2 }
File.write("meta.yml", YAML.dump(data))
Dir Operations: Dir.glob matches file paths with glob patterns (*, **, ?, [set]). Dir.mkdir/Dir.delete create/remove directories. Dir.chdir changes working directory. Dir.children/Dir.each_child list directory entries. Dir.exist? checks existence. Dir.mktmpdir (from tmpdir library) creates temp directories. FileUtils provides higher-level operations (cp, mv, rm_rf, mkdir_p).

# Globbing
Dir.glob("*.rb")                    # all Ruby files in current dir
Dir.glob("**/*.json")               # all JSON files recursively
Dir.glob("src/{lib,test}/**/*.{rb,js}")  # multiple patterns

# Directory operations
Dir.mkdir("new_dir") unless Dir.exist?("new_dir")
Dir.chdir("new_dir") { puts Dir.pwd }
Dir.delete("empty_dir")

# Listing
Dir.children(".").each { |f| puts f }
Dir.each_child("src") { |f| puts f }

# Temporary directory
require 'tmpdir'
Dir.mktmpdir do |dir|
  File.write(File.join(dir, "temp.txt"), "temporary")
  # dir auto-deleted on block exit
end

# Using FileUtils for convenience
require 'fileutils'
FileUtils.mkdir_p("a/b/c")       # creates nested dirs
FileUtils.cp("source.txt", "dest.txt")
FileUtils.mv("old.txt", "new.txt")
FileUtils.rm_rf("temp_dir")      # removes recursively

String Methods: Ruby's String class has extensive methods. Key categories: query (empty?, include?, start_with?, end_with?), transformation (upcase, downcase, capitalize, swapcase, reverse, tr, delete, squeeze), splitting/joining (split, join, chars, bytes, lines), trimming (strip, lstrip, rstrip, chomp, chop), padding (center, ljust, rjust), and more. Many have bang (!) versions for in-place modification.

s = "  Hello, World!  "

# Query methods
s.empty?          # false
s.include?("lo")  # true
s.start_with?("  He")  # true
s.end_with?("!")  # false (trailing space)

# Trimming
s.strip           # "Hello, World!"
s.chomp           # "  Hello, World!  " (removes \n)
s.chomp("!")      # "  Hello, World"

# Transformation
s.upcase          # "  HELLO, WORLD!  "
s.downcase        # "  hello, world!  "
s.reverse         # "  !dlroW ,olleH  "
s.squeeze(" ")    # " Hello, World! " (collapse spaces)

# Delete & replace
"hello".delete("l")     # "heo"
"hello".tr("aeiou", "*")  # "h*ll*"
"hello".gsub("l", "L")  # "heLLo"

# Splitting & joining
"a,b,c".split(",")       # ["a", "b", "c"]
["a", "b"].join("-")     # "a-b"
Interpolation & Formatting: Double-quoted strings support #{expression} interpolation for any Ruby expression. Format strings with format/sprintf (C-style % formatting). The % operator formats strings: `"%.2f" % pi`. Concatenation with +, repetition with *. Here documents (<<~) for multi-line strings. Scanning and unpacking with String#unpack.

name = "Ruby"
version = 3.2

# Interpolation
puts "Hello, #{name}!"         # Hello, Ruby!
puts "Version #{version}"      # Version 3.2
puts "2 + 2 = #{2 + 2}"       # 2 + 2 = 4
puts "#{name.upcase}"          # RUBY

# Formatting
format("Pi: %.2f", Math::PI)   # "Pi: 3.14"
sprintf("%<name>s is %<age>d", name: "Alice", age: 30)
"%.2f" % Math::PI              # "3.14"

# Concatenation & repetition
"Hello " + "World"             # "Hello World"
"Ha" * 3                       # "HaHaHa"

# Here document (heredoc)
sql = <<~SQL
  SELECT * FROM users
  WHERE active = true
SQL

# With interpolation
price = 10
receipt = <<~STR
  Total: $#{'%.2f' % price}
STR
Regular Expressions: Regex literals: /pattern/ or %r{pattern}. =~ returns match position (or nil). !~ returns true if no match. match returns MatchData object. Named captures (?<name>pattern) for readable extraction. gsub with block for dynamic replacement. scan returns all matches. match? (Ruby 2.4+) is fastest (no MatchData allocation).

text = "Hello, my email is alice@example.com"

# Match check
puts /email/ =~ text        # 10 (position)
puts text =~ /email/        # 10

# MatchData
match = text.match(/(\w+)@(\w+)\.(\w+)/)
puts match[0]               # "alice@example.com"
puts match[1]               # "alice"
puts match[2]               # "example"
puts match[3]               # "com"

# Named captures
match = text.match(/(?<user>\w+)@(?<domain>[\w.]+)/)
puts match[:user]           # "alice"
puts match[:domain]         # "example.com"

# gsub with block
"hello".gsub(/[aeiou]/) { |v| v.upcase }  # "hEllO"

# scan — find all matches
"a1b2c3".scan(/\d/)        # ["1", "2", "3"]

# Options
/pattern/i     # case-insensitive
/pattern/m    # multiline (. matches newline)
/pattern/x    # extended mode (ignores whitespace)

# match? — fastest (true/false)
puts /ruby/i.match?("I love RUBY")  # true
Encoding: Ruby strings have an encoding attribute (String#encoding). Common encodings: UTF-8, ASCII-8BIT (BINARY), ISO-8859-1. force_encoding changes encoding label without modifying bytes. encode transcodes to another encoding. Encoding.default_internal/external set default encodings. File I/O with encoding prevents garbled text. Encoding::UndefinedConversionError for incompatible conversions.

s = "Hello"
puts s.encoding        # UTF-8 (default)

# Check encodings
puts Encoding.list.size  # ~100+ encodings
puts Encoding.name_list  # ["ASCII-8BIT", "UTF-8", ...]

# force_encoding — just relabels bytes
bytes = "Hello".force_encoding("ASCII-8BIT")
puts bytes.encoding    # ASCII-8BIT

# encode — actual transcoding
utf8 = "Café"
latin1 = utf8.encode("ISO-8859-1")
puts latin1.encoding   # ISO-8859-1

# File I/O with encoding
File.open("file.txt", "r:UTF-8") { |f| f.read }
File.open("file.txt", "w:UTF-8") { |f| f.write("data") }

# Invalid/undefined character handling
"abc\u2600".encode("ASCII", invalid: :replace, undef: :replace)
# "abc?" (replaces unsupported chars with ?)

Minitest & RSpec: Ruby's standard testing library is Minitest (built-in, no install needed). RSpec is the most popular third-party testing framework (BDD-style). Minitest uses assert methods. RSpec uses describe/it/expect syntax. Both support before/after hooks, let helpers, and matchers. Test-driven development is common in the Ruby community.

# Minitest (built-in)
require "minitest/autorun"

class TestCalculator < Minitest::Test
  def setup
    @calc = Calculator.new
  end

  def test_add
    assert_equal 5, @calc.add(2, 3)
  end

  def test_subtract
    assert_equal 1, @calc.subtract(3, 2)
  end
end

# RSpec (gem)
# describe Calculator do
#   subject { Calculator.new }
#
#   describe "#add" do
#     it "adds two numbers" do
#       expect(subject.add(2, 3)).to eq(5)
#     end
#   end
# end
RSpec describe/it/expect: RSpec uses describe (group), it (example), and expect (assertion). subject defines the object under test. let defines memoized helpers. before hooks run setup. Matchers: eq, be, include, match, raise_error, change, respond_to, have_key. Compound matchers: and, or.

# RSpec test
# describe Calculator do
#   subject { Calculator.new }
#
#   describe "#add" do
#     it "adds two positive numbers" do
#       expect(subject.add(2, 3)).to eq(5)
#     end
#
#     it "handles negative numbers" do
#       expect(subject.add(-1, 1)).to eq(0)
#     end
#   end
#
#   describe "#divide" do
#     it "raises error on zero division" do
#       expect { subject.divide(1, 0) }.to raise_error(ZeroDivisionError)
#     end
#   end
# end

# Common matchers
expect(array).to include(3)
expect(string).to match(/pattern/)
expect { obj.call }.to change(Counter, :count).by(1)
expect(obj).to respond_to(:method_name)
expect { code }.to raise_error(SomeError)
Mocking with RSpec: Test doubles isolate code from dependencies. instance_double (verifies methods exist), class_double, spy. allow sets up stubs (return values). expect sets up message expectations (must be called). and_return, and_raise, and_wrap_original. receive_counts matchers: exactly(n), at_least(n), at_most(n).

# Double with verification
db = instance_double("Database", find: nil, save: true)

# Stub
allow(db).to receive(:find).with(1).and_return({id: 1, name: "Alice"})
allow(db).to receive(:find).with(anything).and_return(nil)

# Message expectation (must be called)
expect(db).to receive(:save).with(hash_including(name: "Bob")).once

# Spies (record calls, verify later)
logger = spy("Logger")
allow_service_call(logger)
expect(logger).to have_received(:log).with(/completed/).at_least(:once)

# Partial mocking for existing instances
allow(File).to receive(:read).and_return("mocked content")

yield & Blocks: yield calls the block passed to a method. block_given? checks if a block was provided. Blocks can receive arguments. The & prefix captures a block as a Proc parameter. Blocks are closures — they capture the surrounding scope. Use {} for single-line blocks, do/end for multi-line.

# yield with arguments
def measure(label)
  start = Time.now
  result = yield(label) if block_given?
  elapsed = Time.now - start
  puts "#{label}: #{elapsed}s"
  result
end

measure("sleep") { |l| puts "Measuring #{l}"; sleep(0.1); 42 }

# block_given?
def greet
  if block_given?
    yield "Hello"
  else
    puts "No block given"
  end
end

# &block parameter
def each_with_logging(array, &block)
  array.each do |item|
    puts "Processing: #{item}"
    block.call(item)
  end
end
Proc.new & proc: Proc objects encapsulate blocks. Proc.new and Kernel#proc create Procs. Call with .call, .[], .(), or .yield. Procs have arity (argument count), curry (partial application), and source_location. Proc objects don't enforce argument count — missing args become nil, extra args ignored.

# Creating Procs
p1 = Proc.new { |x| x * 2 }
p2 = proc { |x| x * 2 }
p3 = ->(x) { x * 2 }  # lambda shorthand

# Calling
puts p1.call(5)     # 10
puts p1[5]          # 10
puts p1.(5)         # 10
puts p1.yield(5)    # 10

# Arity
puts p1.arity       # 1 (required args)

# Curry — partial application
mult = proc { |a, b| a * b }
double = mult.curry.call(2)
puts double.call(5)  # 10

# Default — fills with nil
loose = Proc.new { |a, b| [a, b] }
puts loose.call(1).inspect     # [1, nil]
puts loose.call(1, 2, 3).inspect  # [1, 2]
Lambdas vs Procs: Procs and lambdas are closures — blocks of code that capture their surrounding environment. Lambda checks argument count (strict), Proc doesn't. Lambda returns from itself (like a method), Proc returns from the enclosing method. Use lambdas for strict argument checking and predictable return behavior. Use Procs when you need flexible argument handling.

# Block (implicit)
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }

# Block to proc with &
def run_block(&block)
  block.call
end
run_block { puts "Hello" }

# Proc
p = Proc.new { |x| x * 2 }
puts p.call(5)  # 10
puts p[5]       # 10 (shorthand)

# Lambda
l = ->(x) { x * 2 }
puts l.call(5)  # 10

# Difference: argument checking
p = Proc.new { |a, b| [a, b] }
puts p.call(1).inspect     # [1, nil] (fills missing with nil)
puts p.call(1, 2, 3).inspect  # [1, 2] (ignores extra)

l = ->(a, b) { [a, b] }
# l.call(1)  # ArgumentError (wrong number)
# l.call(1, 2, 3)  # ArgumentError

# Difference: return behavior
def test_proc
  p = Proc.new { return "from proc" }
  p.call
  "from method"
end
def test_lambda
  l = -> { return "from lambda" }
  l.call
  "from method"
end
puts test_proc    # "from proc"
puts test_lambda  # "from method"

# When to use each
# Lambda: callbacks, strict APIs, predictable control flow
# Proc: DSLs, flexible argument handling, block storage
Closures & Binding: Blocks, Procs, and Lambdas are closures — they capture local variables from the surrounding scope. Binding encapsulates execution context. eval with a binding evaluates code in that context. Proc#binding returns the Binding. Closures keep captured variables alive as long as the Proc exists.

# Closure — captures local variables
def make_counter
  count = 0
  proc { count += 1 }
end

counter = make_counter
puts counter.call  # 1
puts counter.call  # 2
puts counter.call  # 3

# Binding
def get_binding
  x = 10
  y = 20
  binding
end

b = get_binding
puts eval("x + y", b)  # 30
puts b.local_variables # [:x, :y]

# Binding from Proc
my_proc = proc { |n| n * multiplier }
multiplier = 5
puts my_proc.binding.eval("multiplier")  # 5

send/define_method: send dynamically invokes methods by name (including private ones). public_send only calls public methods. define_method dynamically defines methods at runtime. These are core metaprogramming tools. send can call any method — use with caution. define_method creates methods that capture surrounding scope (closures).

# Dynamic invocation with send
obj = "hello"
puts obj.send(:upcase)       # "HELLO"
puts obj.send(:include?, "ll")  # true

# send can call private methods
class Secret
  private
  def hidden; "secret!"; end
end
puts Secret.new.send(:hidden)  # "secret!" (bypasses privacy)

# public_send respects privacy
# Secret.new.public_send(:hidden)  # NoMethodError

# Dynamic method definition
class Dynamic
  %w[hello hi hey].each do |greeting|
    define_method(greeting) do |name|
      "#{greeting.capitalize}, #{name}!"
    end
  end
end

d = Dynamic.new
puts d.hello("Alice")  # "Hello, Alice!"
puts d.hi("Bob")       # "Hi, Bob!"

# define_method with closure
class Attribute
  def self.attr_with_default(name, default)
    define_method(name) do
      instance_variable_get("@#{name}") || default
    end
    define_method("#{name}=") do |value|
      instance_variable_set("@#{name}", value)
    end
  end
end
method_missing: method_missing is called when Ruby can't find a method. Override it for dynamic dispatch, proxy patterns, and DSLs. Always override respond_to_missing? to maintain respond_to? consistency. Use super for the default behavior. method_missing is slower than regular method calls — cache results when performance matters.

class DynamicProxy def initialize(target) @target = target end def method_missing(name, *args, &block) if @target.respond_to?(name) @target.send(name, *args, &block) else super # raise NoMethodError end end def respond_to_missing?(name, include_private = false) @target.respond_to?(name, include_private) || super end end proxy = DynamicProxy.new([1, 2, 3]) puts proxy.length # 3 (delegated to Array) puts proxy.respond_to?(:length) # true # Builder DSL example class HtmlBuilder def method_missing(tag, *content, **attrs, &block) attrs_str = attrs.map { |k, v| " #{k}='#{v}'" }.join inner = block ? block.call : content.first "<#{tag}#{attrs_str}>#{inner}" end end h = HtmlBuilder.new puts h.div("Hello", class: "main") #
Hello
DSL Patterns: Ruby's flexible syntax enables internal DSLs (Domain-Specific Languages). Common techniques: instance_eval/class_eval to change self, block-based configuration, method_missing for dynamic builders, define_method for generating methods. Gems like RSpec, Sinatra, and Rails use these patterns extensively.

# Block-based configuration DSL
class Config
  attr_accessor :host, :port, :debug

  def self.configure(&block)
    config = new
    config.instance_eval(&block)
    config
  end

  def set(key, value)
    send("#{key}=", value)
  end
end

config = Config.configure do
  set :host, "localhost"
  set :port, 8080
  self.debug = true
end

# Sinatra-style DSL
class Router
  class << self
    def routes
      @routes ||= []
    end

    def get(path, &handler)
      routes << { method: "GET", path: path, handler: handler }
    end

    def post(path, &handler)
      routes << { method: "POST", path: path, handler: handler }
    end
  end
end

class MyApp < Router
  get "/" do
    "Home page"
  end

  post "/users" do
    "Create user"
  end
end

Threads & Fibers: Thread.new creates OS-level threads (parallel execution). Fibers are lightweight concurrency primitives (cooperative, not parallel). Fiber.yield pauses execution, fiber.resume continues. Threads share memory (use Mutex for safety). Fibers are useful for generators, async-like patterns, and managing stateful iteration.

# Threads
threads = 5.times.map do |i|
  Thread.new do
    sleep(rand(0.1))
    puts "Thread #{i}"
  end
end
threads.each(&:join)  # wait for all threads

# Mutex for thread safety
mutex = Mutex.new
counter = 0
10.times.map do
  Thread.new do
    mutex.synchronize { counter += 1 }
  end
end.each(&:join)
puts counter  # 10

# Fibers
fiber = Fiber.new do
  puts "Fiber: step 1"
  Fiber.yield(1)
  puts "Fiber: step 2"
  Fiber.yield(2)
  puts "Fiber: done"
  3
end

puts fiber.resume  # step 1, returns 1
puts fiber.resume  # step 2, returns 2
puts fiber.resume  # done, returns 3
Rake Tasks: Rake is Ruby's build tool (Rakefile). task defines a task with name and optional dependencies. namespace groups tasks. desc adds description for `rake -T`. Rake supports file tasks, file lists, and shell commands. Common tasks: db:migrate, test, assets:precompile. rake -T lists available tasks.

# Rakefile
desc "Say hello"
task :hello do
  puts "Hello from Rake!"
end

desc "Build project"
task build: [:clean, :compile] do
  puts "Build complete"
end

task :clean do
  rm_rf "build"
end

task :compile do
  mkdir_p "build"
  sh "gcc src/main.c -o build/app"
end

# Namespace
namespace :db do
  desc "Run migrations"
  task :migrate do
    puts "Running migrations..."
  end

  task :seed do
    puts "Seeding data..."
  end

  task setup: [:migrate, :seed]
end

# Run with: rake build
# List tasks: rake -T
# With args: rake db:setup
Sinatra Overview: Sinatra is a lightweight web framework. Routes match HTTP methods and paths. Params hash contains query/form data. Views use Tilt (ERB, Haml, etc.). Middleware with use. before/after filters. Sessions managed with enable :sessions. Sinatra is ideal for small APIs, microservices, and prototyping.

require 'sinatra'

# Routes
get '/' do
  'Hello, Sinatra!'
end

get '/hello/:name' do
  "Hello, #{params[:name]}!"
end

post '/users' do
  content_type :json
  { status: 'created', name: params[:name] }.to_json
end

# Before/after filters
before do
  content_type :html
end

after do
  puts "Request processed"
end

# Templates (create views/index.erb)
get '/template' do
  @title = "Sinatra App"
  erb :index
end

# Configuration
configure do
  set :port, 4567
  enable :sessions
end

# Run with: ruby app.rb
# Or for production: gem install puma && bundle exec puma app.rb
